#6494. The U.S. just lost its measles elimination status. What now?

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The virus, eliminated in 2000, has now been circulating for more than a year

Flyers provide information about a Pennsylvania Department of Health measles vaccination clinic in Lancaster County aiming to curb an ongoing outbreak.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

After two years with nearly 100 measles outbreaks, thousands sickened and nearly a dozen deaths, the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status.

The highly contagious disease is now endemic in the United States, the Pan American Health Organization declared November 17. Analyses of cases dated from when the first outbreak began in 2025 in West Texas through part of 2026 revealed the virus has been spreading uninterrupted for more than a year. That benchmark signals measles is no longer under control.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The United States is not alone. Mexico and Bolivia also lost their measles elimination status, PAHO announced; Canada had lost it in 2025. “Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination coverage,” PAHO director Jarbas Barbosa said in a Nov. 17 news conference. “And this global trend is also affecting the Americas.” Countries will need to not only stop ongoing outbreaks, but also prove that no one caught measles within their borders for a full year to regain measles-free status.

That won’t happen overnight. But there is a way, experts say. Vaccinating people across the country, particularly in areas with low vaccination rates, will stifle the virus’s spread. But so far, the U.S. federal public health response has taken a back seat to efforts from state and local health departments to curb ongoing outbreaks.

Measles’s return “is an enormous black eye on the reputation of the United States,” said epidemiologist Jennifer Nuzzo of the Brown University School of Public Health in Providence, R.I., in a Nov. 9 webinar hosted by the university. The Americas led the global campaign to control the virus, and in 2016 the region became the first to eliminate measles transmission from all its countries.

“To lose [elimination status] means we’re going backwards… meaning decades of progress lost,” Nuzzo said. “It’s an indicator of our lack of protection. It is an indicator of our lack of preparedness for disease threats in general.”

PAHO’s verdict comes amid a surge of measles not seen in the United States since 1991. Health officials have recorded more than 7,000 cases since the beginning of the West Texas outbreak. That tally includes nearly 2,300 measles cases in 2025 and 5,412 in 2026 as of November 12, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Over 90 percent of cases have been in people who are unvaccinated or whose status is unknown. States report that 13 people have died, although the CDC so far recognizes only nine of those deaths.

While mild measles symptoms include high fever, cough and a rash, roughly 1 in 5 people will be hospitalized with complications such as pneumonia or brain swelling. Children younger than 5 years and adults over 20 are more likely to get sick, as are pregnant women and their infants. At least 13 babies were born infected, called congenital measles, since the beginning of 2025, researchers report November 16 in NEJM Evidence. Those babies are at risk for developing dangerous brain swelling that is almost always fatal later on in life.

The measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine helped eliminate measles from the United States in 2000. After that, cases still sometimes popped up. Those cases were mostly in unvaccinated people traveling from parts of the world where the virus still widely circulates. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks.

But widespread misinformation, including a disproven claim that the vaccine causes autism, means fewer children are receiving the MMR shot and more people are questioning its safety. According to the CDC, roughly 92 percent of kindergarteners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in 2025, down from 95 percent in 2019. And in 2025, 83 percent of U.S. adults viewed the MMR vaccine as safe, down from 86 percent in 2024, according to a survey from the University of Pennsylvania’s Annenberg Public Policy Center. Yet decades of evidence show the vaccine is safe and highly effective.

That measles made a comeback is not a surprise, says Nathan Lo, an infectious diseases physician and epidemiologist at Stanford University School of Medicine. Until recently, outbreaks were largely isolated to communities with low vaccination rates and quickly contained. But now, outbreaks seem to be more likely to spill over into neighboring communities, Lo says. “There’s a lot of potential connectedness between the outbreaks.”

What’s more, some infected people aren’t getting tested, making them invisible to officials who are now struggling to trace chains of transmission. An outbreak that hit Arizona and Utah, for instance, was far larger than official numbers suggest, researchers reported July 15 in a preprint at medRxiv.org. The roughly 1,000 confirmed cases may represent just 20 to 30 percent of the outbreak’s true size.

A functional surveillance system is crucial to keeping outbreaks under control, Jonathan Temte, a family medicine physician at the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health in Madison, said in the Brown University webinar. Without good surveillance across the entire country, “we can miss pockets out there if people aren’t reporting, if people are hiding cases.”

But surveillance alone won’t stop the virus from “popcorning across the country,” Nuzzo said. “Measles has returned, and it’s going to take vaccination to stop it.”

Over the last two years, measles outbreaks have popped up across the United States, sickening thousands of people since mid-January 2025. Most of those cases, shown by county where they were reported, are in people who are unvaccinated. Colors on the map indicate the relative number of cases reported. Green represents the lowest and red the highest number of cases. Notable outbreaks have appeared in Utah, Arizona, Texas, South Carolina, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania.

Michael Mitchell and Andrea Uhlig/Brown University School of Public Health

Efforts to boost vaccine uptake could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles, but not all. “Figuring out which ones are [high risk] can be a little tricky,” Lo says. “But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”

Homing in on school districts or individual schools could also help. State health departments typically report vaccination rates among school-age children by county. But that broad metric can hide high risk schools with low vaccination rates, epidemiologists Siyu Chen and Ana Bento reported in August in Nature Medicine. Computer simulations relying on data that included 50,000 schools across the United States showed that school-level estimates best revealed where the virus could gain a foothold. That was true even if county-level vaccination rates were close to 95 percent.

Another element that influenced where measles took off was whether communities with cases were near other areas with low vaccination rates, the team found. The outbreak in Texas, for instance, may have ended faster because communities with low vaccination rates were farther away from one another compared with outbreaks in South Carolina and Pennsylvania, says Bento, of Cornell University. Neighboring areas where many are unvaccinated may face longer-burning outbreaks. “Which is what we are now seeing,” Bento says.

Measles elimination status can be regained. The declaration that the virus is endemic is “not a punishment,” Bento says. It’s a sign that something needs to change. That might include vaccine catch-up campaigns, community outreach or getting rid of nonmedical vaccine exemptions.

Local public health officials are “doing every last thing that you can imagine with limited resources,” health psychologist Noel T. Brewer said in a Nov. 12 webinar hosted by the Association of Health Care Journalists. But a cohesive plan at the federal level could bolster defenses before the virus arrives in new states, noted Brewer, of the University of North Carolina Gillings School of Global Public Health in Chapel Hill.

Such efforts could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles. “A subset [with low vaccination rates] are high risk,” Lo says. “Figuring out which ones are which can be a little tricky. But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”

There’s also wiggle room in the childhood vaccine schedule to provide kids extra protection. Normally children don’t get their first MMR dose until their first birthday. But doctors can give infants an extra MMR dose at 6 months if there is an active outbreak in their area. Pediatricians can also offer the second dose a month after the first one, rather than waiting until around the time children start kindergarten. Adults, particularly those who received only one dose, can also get a booster. It’s unclear whether health officials will officially recommend such actions.

“The problem is that there’s no trusted source for this vaccine decision anymore,” Lo says. Previous vaccine recommendations were up to the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, which was disbanded in March after lawsuits blocked appointments made by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. “Now, there’s a lot of different medical societies and initiatives to try and fill that void,” Lo says. But it’s unclear which would be best positioned to lead.

CDC director Erica Schwartz has said the health agency will not be changing its response to ongoing outbreaks. “We’re going to be doing the same exact thing that we’ve been doing today, which is working with the states,” she told Reuters. The CDC did not respond to Science News requests for an interview, but shared in a Nov. 17 statement that the agency will “encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection.”

Eliminating measles again will take dedicated resources and more funding funneled to public health departments across the country, Lo says. “You see increasing measles outbreaks and a lot of time and resources to contain these outbreaks at a time where you’re slashing budgets,” Lo says, “that’s a really bad mismatch.”

Public health responses to measles are expensive. Officials in New Mexico spent an estimated $5.4 million — over $53,000 per case — responding to a 2025 outbreak that was linked to West Texas. The CDC has provided an additional $100 million to states to help fight measles.

Other countries have beaten back measles after an unwelcome return. Extensive vaccination campaigns helped Venezuela and Brazil regain measles elimination status after briefly losing it in 2017 and 2019. The Public Health Agency of Canada also announced that its nearly two-year-long outbreak officially ended in October, though it’s unclear when the country might earn its status back.

“It is not hopeless,” Nuzzo said. “It can be done, and I hope it will be done [in the United States].”

#6493. A man sees his cat’s eyes in other people’s faces after brain surgery

A rare case report describes a man who sees his cat's eyes in human faces after brain surgery, showing how memory can shape face distortions.

On some days, a 28-year-old man identified as Karl sees his cat’s eyes in every human face he looks at. The researchers who documented his case think the features may come from visual memory.

The case, described in a short report in the journal Cortex, points to how face perception is built.

The features Karl sees are not generic cat eyes. He recognizes them as his own cat’s.

The authors read that as evidence that memory can feed individual facial features back into what a person sees.

The report covers a single case, written up from Karl’s own descriptions, and its images are reconstructions he helped refine rather than scans of anything in his brain.

Brad Duchaine of Dartmouth College led the report with Antônio Mello, a doctoral student at Dartmouth, and Jennifer Nosker, a neuropsychologist at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston.

“This case of Karl seeing his cat’s features in human faces and vice versa demonstrates that individual features can be pulled from memory and influence our ongoing perception,” Duchaine said.

Karl’s distortions began two years ago, after surgeons removed a tangle of blood vessels from the back of his right temporal lobe, a region central to recognizing faces.

The condition is called prosopometamorphopsia, or PMO, in which faces look distorted. His version includes palinopsia, in which something seen earlier persists in later vision.

His gray tabby, Luna, is often the first face he sees in the morning. On those days, her enlarged pupils, cat-like eye sockets, and the shading around them can appear on human faces for hours afterward, in person or on a screen.

The transfer runs the other way too. If a familiar person is the first face he sees, that person’s eye shape and pupil size can show up in his cat’s face. Episodes often last several hours, and occasionally they last the whole day.

What makes the case useful to researchers is the precision of the swap.

Only parts of a face move, usually the eye region, sometimes with its coloring and texture, while the rest of the viewed face looks normal.

The transferred features also look coherent. They blend into the face rather than appearing superimposed on it, and they shift naturally as Karl changes his angle or distance.

And Karl can say whose they are. He identifies the borrowed eyes as belonging to particular people he knows, or to his cat, which led the authors to suggest the features are retrieved from long-term visual memory.

He has frequently experienced human-to-human transfers as well.

The report opens with a case the same journal published in 1986. Nine months after a stroke, a woman riding a bus looked at a poodle on a passenger’s lap, then looked away, and saw the poodle’s face on every passenger.

The poodle faces persisted for about 30 minutes after she got off the bus.

The 1986 case suggested faces are processed differently from other things people see, because the dog’s face appeared only on other faces.

Karl’s experience sharpens the point: the brain seems to store and reactivate identity-specific pieces of faces, not only whole faces.

Whole-face substitutions like the poodle case are rare, the authors wrote.

Over five years, about 275 people reporting face distortions have contacted the lab through its PMO website, and most describe changes to the shape, position, color, or texture of features.

The 1986 case came with a line drawing. Karl’s came with photorealistic images, generated with an AI model from his verbal descriptions and from a sketch he drew.

The images were then refined over several months until he judged they matched his experience. Karl made some of the changes himself.

“AI provides researchers like us with the ability to generate more accurate visualizations of what people are experiencing when they’re having distorted visual perceptions,” Duchaine said.

“If you know what the person is experiencing, you can much better research what they’re dealing with and try to figure out ways to control it.”

The images also help patients explain the condition to family and friends, he added.

Duchaine said his lab has heard from people who were told they had a psychiatric problem, and in some cases were put on antipsychotic drugs, when their problem was visual.

The report rests on one person’s account of his own perception, which no one else can see directly. It is a clinical description, not an experiment, and it does not test what triggers an episode.

What the report can’t say is how common this feature-level borrowing is.

The authors wrote only that several other people with PMO have told them of face palinopsia, against a far larger number who report seeing faces warp in shape or color.

The team plans to keep working with Karl, and the authors expect photorealistic reconstructions to become an increasingly valuable tool for recording what patients with perceptual disorders actually see.

The full study was published in the journal Cortex.

#6492. NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson loses reelection in North Carolina

NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson, right, here at a hearing in June, lost his reelection bid in North Carolina's 9th District. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

North Carolina Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee, has lost his race for reelection, a stinging defeat for the man charged with preserving the House majority for the GOP.

Hudson fell to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator who was leading  51 percent to 49 percent Thursday afternoon  when The Associated Press called the race in North Carolina’s 9th District.

Hudson had already conceded the race Wednesday, when it became clear that his path to victory was closing off.

“[The] voters of North Carolina’s 9th District made their choice and I respect it,” he said in a statement. “Since 2013 I’ve worked for North Carolina families. That includes the soldiers and families at Fort Bragg, who sacrifice more for this country than most people will ever know.”

Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose his seat during a midterm election this decade. In 2022, New York Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney lost reelection while serving as chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

Republicans across North Carolina experienced devastating losses on election night. As of Thursday afternoon, Democrats had also flipped the seats of Reps. Addison McDowell, Brad Knott and Tim Moore, as well as the open seat of retiring Rep. Chuck Edwards. The races for five other GOP-held seats remain uncalled, while Democratic Rep. Don Davis was reelected despite being targeted for defeat under a new GOP-drawn congressional map. Republicans also lost control of the North Carolina House and lost seats in the state Senate.

North Carolina’s 9th District, which includes the Eastern Piedmont region and the Fayetteville area, was far from the House battlefield for much of the midterm cycle. President Donald Trump carried the seat by 16 points in 2024, according to calculations by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales, and Hudson won a seventh term the same year by nearly 19 points. Hudson also held a financial advantage over Ojeda, raising $4.2 million to Ojeda’s $2.9 million through mid-October.

But in the waning weeks of the campaign, signs of Republican concern grew and Hudson’s campaign began spending on ads.

Ojeda was first elected to the West Virginia Senate in 2016. He ran for the U.S. House two years later as a Trump-voting Democrat but lost that race to Republican Carol Miller. He then briefly ran for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination and also challenged GOP Sen. Shelley Moore Capito later that cycle but lost in the Democratic primary.

Ojeda moved to North Carolina in 2020, he told CityView, a local magazine, and he announced his challenge to Hudson last year.

Throughout the campaign, he attacked the incumbent over his support for Trump’s agenda, particularly the war in Iran. Ojeda is a retired Army major and the district is home to Fort Bragg, the nation’s largest Army base by population, where the Democrat was previously stationed for more than a decade.

“We did the impossible,’’ Ojeda told supporters Tuesday night. “We took on the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, a man with political connections, the billionaire donors, and the entire Washington establishment standing beside him.”

Hudson, 55, is finishing his seventh term in the House and his second term as NRCC chair. He had no primary opponent this year and had grown used to winning reelection by comfortable margins.

As a legislator, Hudson focused much of his policy agenda on health issues such as federal pandemic preparedness programs. He serves on the House Energy and Commerce Committee and chairs the panel's Communications and Technology Subcommittee.

Researchers have zeroed in on a genetic variant in the human brain that came from Neanderthals, and it might protect us from schizophrenia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A newfound genetic variant inherited from Neanderthals may shrink a part of modern-human brains without having any meaningful effects on mental ability, and it might also reduce the risk of schizophrenia, a new study finds.

"Genetic differences between Neanderthals and modern humans still influence our brains today," study co-author Hugo Zeberg, an evolutionary geneticist at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Germany, told Live Science. Zeberg and his colleague Svante Pääbo detailed their findings Nov. 16 in the journal PNAS.

Before they went extinct around 40,000 years ago, Neanderthals were among the closest relatives of modern humans. More than a decade of research has shown that Neanderthals and modern humans once interbred. Most people not of sub-Saharan ancestry living today possess about 2% Neanderthal ancestry.

Neanderthals' skulls were larger and more elongated than modern humans'. One reason for the differences has to do with the occipital lobe, the smallest of the brain's four lobes, which sits in the back of the skull. The occipital lobe houses the visual cortex, which helps process signals from the eyes. This area was relatively larger in Neanderthals than it is in modern humans.

In the new study, the researchers analyzed modern-human genomes for genetic variants that are related to occipital lobe size and were also likely inherited from Neanderthals. They discovered one such variant associated with the DAAM1 gene, which a 2019 study linked with brain development. This genetic variant was found only in modern humans outside Africa and was seen in five Neanderthal genomes.

Curiously, the Neanderthal variant the scientists detected in modern-human genomes led to an approximately 0.05-cubic-inch (0.85 cubic centimeters) reduction in occipital lobe size per copy of the variant in an individual. This means that the Neanderthal gene was linked to a slightly smaller brain size in modern humans.

A Neanderthal variant can have a relatively strong effect on brain anatomy without affecting intelligence, while also reducing schizophrenia risk.

This effect is the opposite of what experts expected based on Neanderthals' large skull size, Tony Capra, an evolutionary geneticist at the University of California, San Francisco, who was not involved in the research, told Live Science.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

However, it's important to remember that this one gene variant "does not reflect the full set of variations that might have been present in Neanderthals that might have affected the shape and size of their brain structures," Capra noted.

Zeberg and Pääbo also discovered that having two copies of the DAAM1 gene variant was associated with a nearly 10% reduction in the chances of having schizophrenia in modern humans. But there was no apparent link between the variant and intelligence in modern humans.

"A Neanderthal variant can have a relatively strong effect on brain anatomy without affecting intelligence, while also reducing schizophrenia risk," Zeberg said.

Symptoms of schizophrenia can include altered perceptions of reality, such as visual hallucinations and problems with processing visual signals. This makes it "tempting to speculate" that this Neanderthal gene variant's effects on schizophrenia might be associated with the visual cortex. However, there is currently no evidence for such a link, Zeberg said.

Future research along these lines could analyze how other Neanderthal genetic variants influenced modern humans, Capra said, "to see if they had a consistent effect on us." Looking into Neanderthal variants that are missing from modern-human genomes could "show us what makes us modern humans as opposed to them," Capra added.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Zeberg, H., & Pääbo, S. (2026). A Neandertal-derived genetic variant reduces occipital brain volume in present-day humans. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 123(48). https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2624837123

#6490. A single drop of coolant could change how data centers cool their chips

Low-cost water handles steady heat and one costly coolant drop boils on the spikes, a data center cooling idea tested on a chip at Waterloo.

Cooling an overheating computer chip sounds like a job for more cold liquid. In a lab test, a single drop of coolant cooled a simulated chip’s hottest spot faster than a bath of the same coolant.

Engineers placed the drop, just over a quarter of an inch across, on a heated sapphire square submerged in water.

The drop boiled, and within 15 seconds the center of the hot spot had cooled by about 31°F (17°C).

The idea is to spend expensive coolant only where and when a chip needs it, and let low-cost water do the rest.

Sushanta Mitra, a professor of mechanical and mechatronics engineering at the University of Waterloo in Canada, led the work with postdoctoral researcher Tian-Yu Zhang and doctoral student Arnav Banerjee.

The test ran on a heated square of sapphire standing in for a chip, not on a working processor.

“It’s a division of labor,” said Mitra. “Water is excellent at handling steady, everyday heat and the drops take care of sudden spikes.”

Operators of data centers increasingly cool their servers by submerging the electronics in a liquid that doesn’t conduct electricity.

The trouble is that chips don’t heat evenly. AI workloads have pushed data centers toward denser processors that draw more power.

A processor core can run far hotter than the rest of the chip for a few seconds at a time. Such bursts make chips slow down and age faster, and a liquid that simply surrounds the chip responds slowly.

Coolants that boil pull heat away faster, but they’re costly, and boiling is hard to start at exactly the right spot.

Purified water moves heat better than the standard fluids, and with the electronics insulated it can serve as a coolant itself. In still water, though, the currents that carry heat away from a sudden hot spot can be slow to start.

The sapphire square measured 1.2 inches (30 millimeters) on each side and was thinner than a dime. An electric current heated a coating on its surface.

The chip sat under about 1 fluid ounce (30 milliliters) of purified water, less than half an inch deep.

The team squeezed a drop of Novec-7100, an electronics coolant that boils at about 142°F (61°C), onto the chip through a needle. The coolant is heavier than water and barely dissolves in it, so the drop stayed on the chip.

Then they switched on the power. The highest of three settings was about 86 watts, roughly a bright old-style light bulb’s heat packed into an area the size of a postage stamp.

An infrared camera under the chip recorded its temperature 30 times a second, and a high-speed camera filmed the bubbles. Each test ran three times.

For comparison, the team also ran the chip in a tank of pure coolant and in water alone.

At the highest heat setting, the drop made the difference.

Once the chip’s surface passed the coolant’s boiling point, bubbles formed inside the drop while the water around it stayed liquid. Within 15 seconds, the center of the hot spot was some 31°F (17°C) cooler.

A chip in a tank of pure coolant reached a similar peak temperature, but cooled far more slowly afterward. In water alone, the chip kept getting hotter.

“Boiling soaks up a lot of heat and the rising bubbles stir the surrounding water so it carries heat away faster,” said Mitra, who is also executive director of the Waterloo Institute for Nanotechnology.

“We get the punch of boiling, but only where and when it’s needed.”

The chip surface around the drop also ran cooler than it did in water alone, so the drop was helping beyond the patch it covered.

The boiling drop had limits. At the lowest heat setting, water alone kept the chip coolest early on. And until the drop had boiled away, its own footprint ran up to 29°F (16°C) hotter than the surface around it.

Mitra’s lab specializes in wrapping one liquid in a thin skin of another, and the team tried it on the coolant drops.

The team floated a small ring from a plumbing supplier on the water, poured a thin layer of silicone oil inside it, and let coolant drip through the oil. Each drop picked up a silicone skin as it sank to the chip.

The silicone skin changed the boiling. At the middle heat setting, a plain silicone skin delayed boiling by about 1.5 seconds and let the hot spot climb about 14°F (8°C) higher first.

When boiling did start, it happened all at once, as one large bubble, and that drop cooled the chip faster than any other.

Mixing tiny particles of a heat-conducting ceramic, aluminum nitride, into the oil did the opposite. The particles gave bubbles places to start, so many small bubbles formed instead of one big one.

At the highest heat, those skins cut the peak hot-spot temperature by about 18°F (10°C).

Skins have a cost, though. Leftover oil on the chip surface slowed cooling later on, so the wrapped drops did worse than bare ones over a longer period.

Everything so far happened in still water on a heated square of sapphire, not on a processor in a working server.

Real cooling systems usually pump their liquid, and the authors wrote that boiling in flowing water may behave quite differently and needs its own tests.

High-heat runs also varied noticeably from one repeat to the next, though the overall pattern held each time.

Mitra’s team described two ways the idea could work. Sensors could detect a hot spot and deliver a drop to it, or wrapped drops could circulate in the water and boil wherever they land on something hot enough.

Next on the authors’ list are shell liquids that leave less residue, ways to wrap drops inside flowing coolant, and tests under realistic operating conditions.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Colloid and Interface Science.

#6489. What a city’s sewage can reveal about the health of the people upstream

Eight Ohio cities' sewage carried gut bacteria whose mix lined up with local obesity, blood pressure, and stroke rates, a pilot study finds.

During the pandemic, health departments learned to read a city’s sewage for the virus behind COVID-19.

The same water carries something else from every household that flushes into it: the bacteria living in people’s guts.

In eight Ohio cities, the mix of those gut bacteria in the sewage lined up with how the cities scored on chronic disease.

Cities with more of one group of bacteria that produce hydrogen sulfide had higher rates of obesity, high blood pressure, stroke, and several other conditions.

The study rests on 27 samples collected over seven weeks in May and June 2022, and the authors wrote that the links do not show cause.

What they show is that a sample from a treatment plant can carry a readable signal about the health of the people upstream.

Emma Lancaster, then a doctoral student in the College of Public Health at Ohio State University, led the study with Jiyoung Lee, professor and chair of environmental health sciences.

Lancaster is now an environmental health consultant in Boston.

“During the pandemic, the world learned how to use wastewater to track infectious disease. We asked, what else can it tell us?” Lancaster said.

Sewage arriving at a treatment plant is a blend of everything a community has flushed.

One earlier study the authors cite found up to 97% of the microbes in human stool in untreated sewage.

So the water is a pooled sample of a whole population’s gut bacteria, collected without asking anyone to take a test.

Earlier sewage studies elsewhere had tied a community’s bacterial profile to its rates of obesity, high blood pressure, and smoking.

The Ohio team set out to build full gut bacteria profiles for a set of cities and test them against a wide range of health and social measures.

The team collected a liter of untreated wastewater from each of nine treatment plants, on three days in May and June 2022. Two of the plants serve Columbus, the state capital.

The rest serve smaller cities in central and southeastern Ohio: Zanesville, Marysville, Newark, Lancaster, Athens, Circleville, and Marietta.

Together the plants handle sewage from more than 1.3 million people.

The smallest serves about 15,000 and the largest nearly 548,000. So the cities range from small towns to a major metro area.

Four of the cities count as rural under the federal definition the team used, with fewer than 50,000 residents. The other four are urban.

Each sample was processed the same day. The team sequenced a marker gene to identify the bacteria present. Then they kept only those known to live in the human gut, about 37% of what they read.

For the health side, they pulled public estimates for the census tracts inside each plant’s service area, 329 tracts in all.

The CDC’s PLACES database supplied rates of 23 health conditions and behaviors.

The agency’s Social Vulnerability Index supplied the social and economic measures, such as poverty and unemployment.

Each city’s sewage had its own bacterial profile, and the profiles differed enough that the cities could be told apart.

Several of those differences lined up with health. Cities where smoking was more common had more of one large group of bacteria, the Firmicutes.

Cities with less physical activity had more of two genera, Desulfovibrio and Tolumonas.

Desulfovibrio, a genus of bacteria that produce hydrogen sulfide, appeared again and again. Its abundance was associated with eight health measures.

They were high blood pressure, obesity, stroke, mobility disability, chronic kidney disease, coronary heart disease, chronic lung disease, and cancers other than skin cancer.

Studies of patients have found more Desulfovibrio in people with colorectal, stomach, and breast cancers than in healthy people, the authors wrote.

Researchers suspect its hydrogen sulfide may damage cells.

Asthma ran the other way. Cities with more asthma had a less even mix of gut bacteria and less of a genus called Akkermansia, which is widely treated as a marker of a healthy gut.

Social conditions showed up too. Cities with more unemployment had less diverse gut bacteria overall and more Firmicutes.

The four rural cities carried more Desulfovibrio, more Akkermansia, and more of a major group called Bacteroidota than the urban ones.

They also generally had higher rates of the chronic conditions in the dataset.

“In many cases, poor health outcomes are worse in rural areas and to see these distinct indicators of poorer gut microbiome health in these rural areas offers us clues to some of what is driving that,” Lancaster said.

Marysville, an urban city, sat at the healthy end of nearly every measure, with the lowest rates of smoking, depression, unemployment, and poverty among the eight.

“Wastewater offers a unique way to understand the health of whole communities, not just the people who show up in clinics,” Lee said.

Eight cities give eight data points. The authors wrote that their results should be read as exploratory, not as reliable estimates for any one city.

Columbus alone accounts for most of the 1.3 million people, which could tilt comparisons.

The health figures are also modeled estimates for census tracts, not counts of diagnosed patients. And the samples cover seven weeks of one year.

A deeper problem is in the pipes. Desulfovibrio and Acetobacterium live in sewers as well as in guts, and their numbers in wastewater can rise or fall with how long sewage stays in a pipe.

The authors wrote that future studies should record sewer conditions to separate the human signal from the plumbing.

A larger study could test whether the same patterns hold across more cities and over longer periods while accounting for diet, access to health care, and sewer conditions.

Wastewater already tracks viruses such as those behind COVID, flu, and mpox, Lee said.

Tracking a community’s gut bacteria the same way, she said, could eventually show whether a nutrition program is improving its gut health.

The full study was published in the journal Environmental Research.

#6488. Cracks in public health grew in 2026

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Disease outbreaks revealed a weakened federal response

Outbreaks of measles, cyclosporiasis, Ebola and hantavirus exposed a weakened U.S. public health response.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Public health is invisible — until it’s not.

It’s tough to tally the injuries or deaths that don’t happen thanks to seat belts, lead testing, smoking bans and vaccines. “It is the invisibility paradox,” says Georges Benjamin, CEO of the American Public Health Association in Washington, D.C. “We are invisible because when our best work is done, nothing happens.”

But when disaster strikes — say, an outbreak or a pandemic — people take notice. This year’s outbreaks of measles, Ebola, hantavirus and cyclosporiasis brought recent federal reductions into focus — and exposed cracks in a system that aims to keep people healthy. For years, that system functioned “reasonably well” despite chronic underfunding, Benjamin says. “But since the Trump administration has come on board, they have really made the system at all levels much more dysfunctional.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In 2025, the second Trump administration instituted sweeping federal funding cuts and layoffs, dismantled the global health–focused U.S. Agency for International Development and withdrew the United States from the World Health Organization. Officials reversed some of those changes in the wake of lawsuits and public backlash. But the damage persists.

Two stalwarts of U.S. public health — the Food and Drug Administration and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — have lost between 20 and 30 percent of their staff, due largely to layoffs and early retirements. They have had to scale back, pause or cancel crucial disease-tracking programs at home and abroad. Some CDC divisions don’t have enough staff to function. And both agencies have cut funding to the local governments and nonprofits that shoulder much of the nation’s public health work.

Combined with deep cuts to international aid, that has stymied efforts to contain infectious disease outbreaks around the world, with Ebola in particular going undetected for months, public health experts say.

Domestically, 2026 saw a record-breaking measles outbreak, with some 5,412 confirmed cases as of November 12. That’s more than double last year’s count, and it is the highest number of annual cases since 1991. In mid November, the Pan American Health Organization determined that measles is again endemic to the United States and has stripped the country of its elimination status.

Against a backdrop of shifting federal vaccine guidance, fewer children are receiving the MMR shot that prevents measles. Roughly 92 percent of kindergartners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in the 2025–2026 school year, down from 95 percent in the 2019–2020 school year, according to the CDC. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent the measles virus from sparking an outbreak.

“The fact that we are spending so much time and energy [on measles] when we have a reliable vaccine is very disconcerting,” says Lori Handy, a pediatric infectious diseases physician and associate director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia.

The CDC has not responded to Science News requests for an interview.

Such issues do not bode well for the future. Public health is tested during times of crisis, and the world will eventually face another pandemic, says Michael Osterholm, director of the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. “We’ve not responded [to the 2026 outbreaks] in a way that would give me confidence that the public health system … is prepared for what’s coming down the pike.”

On the heels of multiple 2025 outbreaks, measles continued to wallop parts of the United States this year. Communities in South Carolina, Utah and Wisconsin have been among the hardest hit, with sporadic outbreaks also popping up in other states. Until August, however, none of this year’s outbreaks had turned deadly. That all changed in Pennsylvania.

About a quarter of this year’s cases stem from an outbreak in central Pennsylvania, where the virus has spread widely in communities with low vaccination rates. Since April, seven people in the state have died, including two infants too young to be vaccinated. The CDC has so far attributed just six deaths to measles, despite the insistence of Pennsylvania state public health officials. Three children died of measles in November in New York and Wisconsin.

As of November 12, U.S. health officials recorded 5,412 measles cases for 2026. The last time this many cases were recorded was 1991, nearly a decade before the disease was eliminated from the country.

Measles spreads like wildfire, and one sick person can infect more than a dozen others in an unvaccinated community. While milder symptoms include fever and a hallmark full-body rash, infection can lead to pneumonia, brain swelling and even death. Statistically, the virus kills one to three out of every 1,000 infected people.

The United States eliminated measles in 2000, thanks to the MMR vaccine. “Elimination” means the virus was not spreading widely, and any outbreaks were controlled within a year. But dropping vaccination rates have reestablished the conditions to sustain multiple outbreaks — and may have done so as early as 2022, researchers reported in August in Nature Medicine.

In the wake of losing measles elimination status in November, beating back the the virus again “will take a true change in the public’s trust of health care,” Handy says. That means figuring out how to get people vaccinated — and to encourage them to work with public health officials on testing and contact tracing after exposure.

During the 2009–2010 school year, 20 states had MMR vaccination rates equal to or above 95 percent among kindergartners. Just 10 states hit that threshold for 2025–2026, and 18 states had vaccination rates below 90 percent.

It has been more than three decades since measles caused widespread outbreaks in the United States, and many have never experienced the devastation it can cause. When one community hears about an outbreak halfway across the country, “it still feels very foreign,” Handy says. When the threat feels far away, people are not likely to line up to get a vaccine. Yet measles is so contagious that one unvaccinated traveler can bring the virus back home and spark an outbreak in their own community.

Even with the recent spike in cases, there is hope vaccination rates can catch up, says Cornell University epidemiologist Ana Bento. She points to California and New York, which experienced outbreaks in 2015 and 2018; they ended non-medical exemptions for school vaccinations shortly thereafter. Both states now have vaccination rates above 95 percent in kindergartners. “This is not a tipping point where there’s no coming back,” Bento says.

If measles exposed the consequences of long-simmering vaccine hesitancy, then this summer’s cyclosporiasis outbreak was a quick lesson in food safety screening.

In June, Michigan detected its first cases of the foodborne illness. By August 31, contaminated lettuce had caused the largest outbreak of explosive diarrhea ever in the United States, with 12,883 cases reported across 21 states. By the time the CDC declared the outbreak over on September 11, some 570 people had been hospitalized and two had died. Another 8,113 cyclosporiasis infections have not been traced back to any source. “[This] was one of those events where you felt like the cracks showed,” Handy says.

But it isn’t easy to track the origins of foodborne illness. Typically, local and state public health officials report cases to the CDC — and investigate the outbreak, with the agency lending support as needed. If patient interviews reveal the culprit to be produce, dairy or packaged food, the CDC contacts the FDA, which identifies the producer and the distribution area — and coordinates recalls. The FDA also conducts on-the-ground investigations at the farms and processing facilities that supplied the food.

It can take weeks to identify which contaminated foods are behind a foodborne illness outbreak. Each outbreak is different and timing can depend on the pathogen, laboratory evidence and availability of records, an FDA spokesperson told Science News. After Michigan health officials notified CDC that something was amiss on June 25, it was another 21 days before federal officials announced a possible culprit: shredded lettuce ultimately traced to a Taylor Farms processing facility in Mexico.

Of more than 20,000 cyclosporiasis cases reported this year, nearly 13,000 occurred across 21 states, with the preponderance of them in the Midwest.

The FDA aims to complete investigations as soon as possible. But delays in agency reporting early in the investigation led to unnecessary confusion about which foods to avoid in which states, said Sarah Sorscher, director of regulatory affairs at the Washington, D.C.–based Center for Science in the Public Interest, at a July 16 news briefing. “It’s a perfect storm for viral news. A lot of people have been posting on social media about avoiding fruits and vegetables, which is not good public health messaging.”

Sorscher applauded the dedication of public servants working to contain the outbreak. But she said they were working with inadequate support. “These programs are completely overwhelmed by the scale and scope of the work of solving and communicating these novel emerging outbreaks with a dwindling set of resources.”

Due in part to funding squeezes, in 2025 the CDC stopped mandatory surveillance of six foodborne pathogens, including the single-celled parasite that causes cyclosporiasis, Cyclospora. Speaking at the July 16 news briefing, epidemiologist Barbara Kowalcyk of George Washington University’s Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition Security in Washington, D.C., noted that half of CDC’s food safety budget goes to states to support surveillance and other programs. Yet that budget has remained flat for nearly a decade.

FDA investigations have also been impacted, with foreign food inspections at historical lows. In the case of cyclosporiasis, delays gathering testing supplies and getting clearance from the Mexican government meant it took nearly a month for FDA investigators to arrive in Mexico once the source of the outbreak was identified, according to the New York Times. Once there, inspectors found the parasite in a wastewater tank at a Taylor Farms processing plant — and in a drainage ditch at a farm that supplied the lettuce. Since Cyclospora infects only humans, the probable contaminant was sewage from a source that has yet to be identified.

Without knowing the source of the contamination, it’s hard to know how to stop the parasite from reaching produce in the future, says Francisco Diez-Gonzalez, a food microbiologist at the University of Georgia in Athens. “It leaves us with the feeling that we most likely are going to have something similar next year.”

Starting in 2027, FDA plans to increase surveillance of produce historically associated with Cyclospora and boost laboratory capacity in Mexico to speed up investigations.

Outbreaks of other foodborne pathogens — including Salmonella, Listeria and E. coli — have popped up this year, but not at a rate that’s out of the ordinary, says Diez-Gonzalez, who served on the U.S. National Advisory Committee on Microbiological Criteria for Foods before the Trump administration disbanded it in 2025. That suggests the sky isn’t falling, though he and others are concerned about our future ability to quickly contain outbreaks.

“We may see [fewer] cases, but it’s not that they are disappearing,” Diez-Gonzalez says. “We will not be able to detect them because we don’t have the resources.”

When the WHO announced in May that an Ebola outbreak had erupted in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the virus had been simmering for months. People in the mining town of Mongbwalu, where the outbreak was first detected, began falling ill in January or earlier, according to reporting from Science. Armed conflict in the region has made the outbreak response difficult, says the WHO, and some aid workers and health facilities have been attacked.

Confirmed Ebola cases as of November 15, 2026. To date, 5,593 people have died, and 3,109 have recovered

As cases and death counts soared in May, health officials scrambled to test a backlog of patient samples for Bundibugyo virus, the species behind what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak ever recorded. As of November 15, there were 11,432 confirmed cases and 5,593 deaths. Roughly 3,109 people have recovered. Cases have also been detected in France, Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.

Before the outbreak, the United States significantly scaled back international aid that once flowed from USAID and the CDC. Such cuts may have hampered Ebola monitoring before the outbreak was declared — and affected infection control measures such as contact tracing, says infectious disease physician Krutika Kuppalli of UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas.

Kuppalli led an Ebola treatment unit in Sierra Leone during the 2014–2016 outbreak, the largest ever recorded. At the time, the CDC sent 1,450 physicians, epidemiologists and other experts to help out in affected areas. So far around 500 CDC employees stationed in the United States and abroad have responded to the current outbreak.

By September, the U.S. State Department pledged $887 million toward the purchase of personal protective equipment and the building of new Ebola treatment units. That’s roughly a third of the total amount sent during the 2014–2016 outbreak. Still, earlier investments in public health could have saved lives and helped minimize transmission, Kuppalli says.

Information-sharing has also been a huge problem, Kuppalli says. Prior to the second Trump administration, U.S. health officials were in constant contact with WHO teams that shared information about cases and contact-tracing efforts. After the United States withdrew from the WHO in January 2025, CDC officials had to coordinate with other groups such as UNICEF, the United Nations Children’s Fund.

Nevertheless, there has been some progress toward developing treatments and vaccines. Researchers in Congo are testing whether antivirals and engineered antibodies can stave off severe disease and death in people infected with Bundibugyo virus, and whether those treatments can protect people after exposure. In October, a large clinical trial began testing a vaccine that is already approved against the species that caused the 2014–2016 outbreak. Kuppalli and colleagues argued in September in the Lancet Infectious Diseases that the vaccine’s potential for cross-protection merited its use in high-risk situations.

Two Bundibugyo-specific vaccines are poised to join the new trial after early evidence in animals and people showed the shots are safe — and suggested they may be protective.

Conditions have improved in some parts of Congo, according to the WHO. But there are still hundreds of new cases per week, and other countries should be prepared to respond quickly if the virus crosses borders. “The longer this outbreak continues, the more opportunities the virus has to reach new communities,” Kuppalli says.

The M.V. Hondius was in for a rough voyage the moment it set off from Ushuaia, Argentina, on April 1. A passenger on the small ship had contracted Andes hantavirus, a rodent-borne disease that can cause severe respiratory illness and death. By the time the outbreak was contained, 13 people were infected and three people had died. Public health experts say a lagging U.S. response let other countries take the lead — and suggests the country is not prepared for future epidemics.

It’s unclear how the first patient, who died on April 11, was infected. Another patient died on the ship, and a third — who was allowed to board a plane — died in South Africa.

More than 300 high-risk contacts, including people who spent more than 15 minutes with an infected individual, were quarantined and monitored across 33 countries and territories. None of them got sick. Nor did another 336 low-risk contacts who had brief encounters with someone who fell ill, and who monitored themselves for symptoms.

The United States’ severed relationship with the WHO “in many ways hampered the [country’s] hantavirus outbreak response,” says Benjamin, of the American Public Health Association. Before 2025, U.S. experts frequently received information about emerging health threats from the organization. But confusion over who government officials could talk to likely resulted in knowledge gaps and communication delays, Benjamin says. “CDC was not engaged as early on as they needed to be on that outbreak.”

Instead, other countries including Spain, South Africa, Argentina and Chile played leading roles. After scientists in South Africa determined that Andes hantavirus was behind the outbreak on May 2, passengers disembarked in mid-May in Tenerife, Spain, where health officials screened for symptoms and helped people travel home.

“Outbreak response depends on the knowledge and the relationships that already exist.”

The CDC didn’t set up a response team until after May 2, according to the New York Times. And controversy erupted over uneven U.S. quarantine practices, with some people forced to remain for weeks in quarantine units in Omaha, Neb., while others remained at home. “There was nothing standard” about the protocols, Osterholm says. “Almost everybody got a different approach.”

The outbreak, which ended July 2, was quickly contained in part because Andes hantavirus isn’t very contagious. Of more than 50 known hantaviruses, Andes hantavirus is the only one known to spread from person to person. Although some rare superspreaders transmit the virus to others through casual contact, transmission typically happens through close contact, such as spending long periods of time together or kissing. It would have been harder to stop a pathogen that spreads easily through the air, Osterholm says. “By the time that they recognized what was going on, transmission would have already occurred.”

The international collaboration had some successes, says virologist Gustavo Palacios of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City. Experts in South Africa “kept digging when everything was negative,” he says, until they finally identified Andes hantavirus as the cause.

Hantavirus infections are also relatively rare in the Americas, for now. Studies suggest climate change will increase the likelihood that hantaviruses — and other zoonotic illnesses like Ebola — will make the jump from animals to humans. Dense cities can make it easier for diseases to spread. And such threats don’t disappear when funding for studying them dries up.

“The strongest lesson [from the M.V. Hondius] is that outbreak response depends on the knowledge and the relationships that already exist before the event,” Palacios says. Of the billions of viruses on Earth, just a few hundred pose threats to people. With enough resources, researchers can work together to learn as much as possible about those pathogens and be better prepared when a new one emerges — just as previous work on coronaviruses made the rollout of COVID-19 vaccines possible within a year of the pandemic’s start.

“We will not always know in advance which [pathogens] will become important,” Palacios says. But by not tracking rare threats that could one day become larger problems, “we are shooting ourselves in the foot.”

#6487. Dragonfly wings inspired a new way to build materials that can take a hit

Engineers took cues from dragonfly wings to 3D-print materials that spread damage and absorb energy when compressed.

A neat grid or honeycomb looks like the smartest way to build something light and strong, and engineers have borrowed both for decades. Squeeze a printed grid hard enough, though, and it fails the way a stack of cans does.

One row buckles, then the next, in a band that runs across the whole piece.

A leaf’s veins, a dragonfly’s wing and a spider’s web are built the opposite way, from struts of wildly different sizes tangled together.

Materials printed on that plan spread the damage out instead of concentrating it. They also absorbed as much energy as the tidy lattices, or more.

Engineers at MIT and network scientists at Northeastern University’s Network Science Institute designed the new materials, which they call scale-rich metamaterials.

So far the team has tested them as flat, credit-card-sized polymer plates in a lab, not as helmets or packaging.

“This is a completely new way of thinking for metamaterials,” said study author Carlos Portela, associate professor of mechanical engineering at MIT.

Metamaterials get their properties from their internal architecture rather than their chemistry. Engineers usually design one small building block, a unit cell, and repeat it over and over.

So every strut inside is about the same length and thickness.

Albert-László Barabási, a physicist at Northeastern, has spent his career mapping networks from the internet to the brain. Those networks don’t look like a grid at all.

The veins in a dragonfly’s wing run from about four thousandths of an inch (0.1 millimeters) to about two inches (50 millimeters) long.

Leaf veins and spider silk span a range at least as wide, and the struts inside bone vary tenfold in thickness.

Barabási asked whether that spread of sizes could be built into a solid material on purpose. He took the question to Portela’s lab, with a mathematician at Utrecht University in the Netherlands joining the team.

The team’s recipe is short. A computer picks a random point inside a square and draws a straight beam through it at a random angle, until the beam hits the edge.

The computer picks another point and draws another beam, which stops when it meets the first.

Each new beam is thinner than the last, by a rate the designer sets. Only two settings matter: how thick the first beam is and how fast the thickness shrinks.

The program repeats the step hundreds of times, so the last beams are short and fine while the first few stay long and thick.

The finished design has no typical strut. Lengths, thicknesses and the number of crossings per beam all run across orders of magnitude inside one sample, the same pattern network scientists find in road maps and food webs.

Changing those two settings also changes how stiff the material is in different directions. Across 2,600 computer-generated designs, the directional stiffness varied 24-fold.

That is far more range than a square grid, a honeycomb or a random foam-like Voronoi pattern can offer.

The researchers 3D-printed the designs in a stiff polymer. Each sample was a few inches across, with beams from a few thousandths of an inch up to an inch or so long.

Then they squeezed the samples in a press, alongside square, honeycomb and Voronoi samples of the same density, about 42% solid, three of each.

The square grid buckled first in a single row, and the collapse spread sideways across the whole sample before the next row went. The honeycomb formed wide crushed bands.

Even the random Voronoi foam compacted from the bottom up while its top stayed untouched.

The scale-rich samples didn’t do that. Their stress rose smoothly as the press pushed down, with no sudden drops, and the crushing stayed spread across the whole piece.

The team scored that spread on a scale where zero means perfectly even deformation and one means all the damage in one spot.

The new samples stayed at or below 0.2 even after being compressed by 25% of their original height.

The energy they soaked up before packing down matched or beat the three conventional designs.

“Because there is such a richness of length scales in these networked materials, if one part fails, there is a strong web of structures around it that keeps the entire material from failing catastrophically,” Portela said.

“It’s more efficient at distributing damage and absorbing energy.”

For a final test, the team borrowed from the thick, graded rind of a pomelo, denser toward the outside.

They generated a network whose beams crowded the edges and steered load around a disc of clear acrylic embedded in the middle.

Under compression, the acrylic disc inside a square or honeycomb lattice showed bands of stress under polarized light. Inside the scale-rich network, the bands were far fewer.

Computer simulations put the stress on the disc at as little as about one-fifth of the stress in the conventional lattices.

The same two settings can also tune how fast vibrations travel through the material. The team used that to design a lens that focuses sound waves, so far only in simulation.

Everything the team crushed was a flat plate of one polymer, printed at a resolution of about four thousandths of an inch.

The authors showed on paper that the recipe extends to three dimensions, with plates or beams instead of lines. The stiffness trends carry over, but those 3D versions were simulated rather than squeezed.

The study didn’t test the materials as any product. Helmets, armor, packaging and crash parts are the uses the authors named, and each would need its own tests at full size.

The group has posted its generator code publicly. The authors wrote that a design needing only two inputs is well suited to AI-driven searches for structures with a target stiffness or energy absorption.

Future studies could run those searches, and print the 3D versions to see whether the even crushing holds in a solid block.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#6486. At the Races: After the deluge

Tuesday’s rout by Democrats has led one group dedicated to electing more Republican women to Congress to warn of a “crisis-level decline” of female GOP members on Capitol Hill.

Danielle Barrow, the president of Women for Women Action Fund, drew parallels between this week’s results and the 2018 blue wave.

“After 2018, when Republicans lost 40 seats and elected only one new Republican woman, the party made a real commitment to recruiting and investing in women – and it worked,” Barrow said in a statement Wednesday, adding that women accounted for 11 of the 15 House seats the GOP picked up in the 2020 election. But she cautioned that the party needs to sustain that focus across election cycles.

“Republicans cannot only make this investment after a wipeout election and abandon it when things improve,” she said. “It is time for party leaders to treat this as a permanent strategy, not a crisis response.”

The ranks of House Republican women won’t plummet to as low as after the 2018 elections, when the caucus had just 13 female members. At least 18 Republican women have won House races so far, according to The Associated Press, and two others are leading as of Thursday afternoon. The conference is likely to see two new female members: Florida’s Sydney Gruters, the wife of RNC Chairman Joe Gruters, and Washington state’s Amanda McKinney, who holds a comfortable lead as votes continue to be counted.

Still, those figures are worlds apart from House Democrats, whose caucus will have more than 100 women next year.

“We have always known that when women run, women win,” Florida Rep. Lois Frankel, chair of the member-led Elect Democratic Women PAC, said in a statement Wednesday.

Those incoming new members span the ideological range of the party, including progressives from New York and California who scored big primary wins this summer, to more moderate Democrats who flipped seats in Virginia and Pennsylvania.

House Democrats had set a public goal this cycle to push their female membership past 100. Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who is retiring at the end of the year, said electing Democratic women had been her “passion” since she joined the House in 1987.

“We made a decision to make more room for women at the tables of power – and generations of candidates, organizers and supporters have carried that work forward,” she said.

Blue breakthrough: Democrats flipped the House and Senate this week, giving the party one of its biggest nights in decades. On the Senate side, they wrested seats from Republicans in Texas, South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and Ohio, while finally flipping Maine. Meanwhile, on the House side, Democrats were on track to not just win every race rated a Toss-up by Inside Elections but also pick up seats in deep-red territory that weren’t considered competitive until late in the cycle. Mary Ellen and Daniela summed up their initial election night takeaways, including how Democratic moderates and progressives both cheered the results and why many of Trump’s picks flopped at the ballot box.

Not going anywhere: The top Senate Democrat, Charles E. Schumer of New York, is confident he will be elected majority leader by his caucus, especially after the party’s resounding midterm wins. Several of his incoming members have promised to support others, our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports, but the reality is there’s no real plausible alternative. Schumer’s own seat is up in 2028.

Redistricting rout: Republicans’ redistricting gambit hasn’t paid off as they’d hoped, the latest election results show, with the GOP appearing poised to flip only a handful of redrawn seats. Democratic incumbents who sought reelection from their reconfigured seats appeared poised to all win, although the race for Rep. Darren Soto’s Central Florida seat remained uncalled as of Thursday afternoon.

Taking the chair: Among the bruising defeats that North Carolina Republicans suffered this week was National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson’s loss to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator. Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose reelection this decade after New York’s Sean Patrick Maloney , who lost in 2022 while serving as the DCCC chair.

New senators: The incoming Senate Democratic class includes a returning senator, a former governor, two lieutenant governors and a congressman, a notable amount of governing experience. Meanwhile, five Republican House members are moving across the Rotunda after winning open Senate seats.

Member-to-governor pipeline grows: Five newly elected governors will be departing Capitol Hill to become the top executive of their state or territory, Savannah reports. Additionally, two former members who also served in the Biden administration were elected governor, though a trio of House Republicans fell short in their gubernatorial bids.

Comeback season: Roll Call’s Nick Eskow reports on the former members who are poised to return to the House or Senate next year, with at least seven winning comeback bids Tuesday.

The firsts: Several candidates made history this week with their elections to Congress or the governorships of their state. Roll Call’s Andrew Menezes rounds up the milestone wins.

D.C. in the House: Robert White, D.C.’s newly elected nonvoting delegate, told our colleague Nina Heller that he plans to lobby fellow Democrats next year to support D.C. statehood. A potential selling point: The party could tackle affordability concerns better with two Democratic senators from the deep-blue District, he said.

Keeping count: As of 4:30 p.m. Thursday, Democrats had flipped 42 seats in the House and seven in the Senate, according to the AP. Republicans have so far picked up two House seats, both through redistricting. Twenty-eight House contests and two Senate races (Alaska and Mississippi) remain uncalled as of publication time. Check out Roll Call’s results tracker for updates as the races are called.

Indie losses: Independent Senate hopefuls running in deep-red states did not find success on Tuesday, even in races without a Democrat on the ballot. In Nebraska, former union leader Dan Osborn came up short in his second Senate bid. In Idaho, former state legislator Todd Achilles failed to dislodge Sen. Jim Risch, while Navy veteran Brian Bengs couldn’t topple South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds. In Montana, where the Democratic nominee did not drop out, former university president Seth Bodnar lost to Republican Kurt Alme. On the House side, Alaska GOP Rep. Nick Begich comfortably leads commercial fisherman Bill Hill, though below the 50 percent threshold needed to avoid a ranked-choice runoff. With votes still being counted, the AP had yet to call the race at publication time.

Not just Congress: The blue wave that broke Republican majorities on Capitol Hill also washed over state legislatures. Democrats are poised to hold new majorities in 12 legislative chambers, including the North Carolina House and Texas House, according to the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, although some results aren’t official yet. The party also won governing trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Meanwhile, in blue states, Democrats tightened their grip on government: In Rhode Island, Republicans are on track to hold just 10 seats in the entire 113-member legislature, while next door in Connecticut, the 36-seat Senate could have as few as three GOP members.

Blame game: As Republicans take stock of what went wrong for them in the midterms, Vice President JD Vance was quick to point to the Iran conflict as an insurmountable albatross. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance said in a lengthy X post. “If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. … But everyone knows why we lost.”

But the tariffs: A pair of Republican former senators, Arizona’s Jeff Flake and Pennsylvania’s Patrick J. Toomey, both also urged their party to focus on the impact of Trump’s tariff policies. “Arbitrary and capricious tariffs directly raised costs for all American consumers,” Toomey wrote Wednesday on X. “Many voted for Democrats yesterday.”

Staying put: Pennsylvania Rep. Brendan F. Boyle says he will remain in the House, where he’s poised to become the next Budget Committee chair, rather than launch a Democratic primary challenge to Sen. John Fetterman next cycle.

Bayh Bayh Bayh: A third generation of Indiana’s famed Bayh family won political office this week, with Beau Bayh’s election as secretary of state. Bayh, a Marine Corps veteran, follows in the footsteps of his father, Evan Bayh, who won the same post 40 years ago before going on to serve as governor and senator, and his late grandfather, Birch Bayh, who won three terms in the Senate. Indiana Democrats had a breakthrough election this week, defeating GOP Rep. Victoria Spartz, winning a second statewide office, unseating the speaker and breaking the GOP supermajority in the state House.

A win and a loss: Nebraska Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts won reelection, but his wife, Democrat Susanne Shore, lost a special election for a seat on University of Nebraska Board of Regents, which governs the university system. Shore, who lost to a fellow Democrat in the officially nonpartisan race, was making her first bid for elective office.

Bans on the ballot: Voters in Arizona, Nebraska and Washington state have approved new measures barring transgender athletes from participating in girls sports. A similar proposal in Colorado also appears likely to pass, although the AP had yet to call it as of publication time.

Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections shares 15 initial lessons from the midterm elections, from the president’s “political mortality” to candidate quality and the power of personal brands. And, Nathan writes, as bad a night as it was for Republicans, it could have been even worse.

As Maine goes: The New York Times caught up with with Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her bid for a sixth term in Maine. Collins, who had survived tough cycles before, spoke of getting “caught up in the Trump tsunami” and how she finally had her “Margaret Chase Smith moment.”

“These are extinction-level numbers”: Texas Monthly sat down for an interview with former state House Speaker Dade Phelan, who anticipated a down-ballot GOP rout but not the full extent of it. “MAGA needs to be dead,’’ said the Republican, who led the push to impeach state Attorney General Ken Paxton in 2023 and then was targeted for defeat by Trump. He opted against reelection this year.

Corruption a top issue: The Associated Press reported that its 2026 voter poll found corruption at the top of the list of concerns for voters who helped sweep Democrats into power on Capitol Hill.

Tar Heeled: Among the states where Republicans suffered their biggest defeats Tuesday, perhaps none was more stunning than North Carolina, where they've so far lost five U.S. House seats and are trailing in one another and lost control of the state House. The (Raleigh) News & Observer looks at how maps “designed to deliver strong Republican majorities [failed] so spectacularly at that goal.”

Support and discord: Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s sharply critical views toward Israel roiled the Jewish community in Michigan. But exit polling suggests most Jewish voters backed him, albeit in smaller numbers than they might have had a different Democrat run, Religion News Service reports.

That's how many House districts won by Trump in 2024 have been called for Democratic candidates by the AP as of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time on Thursday.

Twenty-eight additional Trump-won districts remain uncalled at publication time, and Democrats are currently leading in eight of those races.

The figures stand in sharp contrast to the start of the cycle, when there were just 13 House Democrats in districts that backed Trump in 2024.

Since then, several Republican-led states redrew their congressional maps in an effort to increase the number of Trump-won districts and improve their party’s chances of holding the House.

In large part, this effort appears to have backfired in 2026, with the Democratic wave cresting high enough to wash over dozens of Trump-won districts. Twenty-one of the 52 Democratic wins so far have come in states that redrew their congressional lines: Texas (six Trump-won seats), North Carolina (six), Ohio (five), Florida (three) and Alabama (one).

Congressional Republicans are holding leadership elections next week as they transition from the majority to the minority party. Speaker Mike Johnson is not seeking his conference’s top post, setting up a clash to be the next House minority leader. On the Senate side, South Dakota’s John Thune hopes to continue leading his party in the chamber.

#6485. Voyager 1's light-day milestone: See the photos behind the discoveries
